learn.hook: A coal miner in Jharia, a fisherwoman in Kerala and a wheat farmer in Punjab share one thing: they earn directly from the earth.
points: Human economic activities are grouped as primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary and quinary.

Primary activities depend directly on the environment and use earth's resources like land, water, vegetation, building materials and minerals: hunting, gathering, pastoral activities, fishing, forestry, agriculture, and mining and quarrying.
People engaged in primary activities are called red-collar workers because of the outdoor nature of their work.
As an economy develops, the share of its workforce in primary activities falls and more people move to secondary and tertiary work.

example.q: Classify: (a) a quarry worker in Rajasthan, (b) a textile mill worker in Surat, (c) a bank clerk in Kolkata.
steps: (a) Quarrying uses earth's resources directly → primary.
(b) Turning cotton into cloth → secondary.
(c) Providing a service → tertiary.

learn.reallife: Over 40% of India's workforce is still in agriculture (PLFS), while in the USA it is under 2% — a clear sign of different development levels.

learn.hook: Ever chewed gum? Its original base, chicle, was gathered from the sap of the Zapota tree in Central America.
points: The earliest humans depended on their immediate environment for food, shelter and clothing; hunting and gathering are the oldest economic activities.
Early hunters used primitive tools made of stones, twigs or arrows; people near coasts also fished.

Gathering is practised in high latitudes (northern Canada, northern Eurasia, southern Chile) and low latitudes (Amazon basin, tropical Africa, northern fringe of Australia and interior parts of South-east Asia).

Modern gathering is market-oriented: bark for quinine, tannin extract and cork; leaves for beverages, drugs and cosmetics; fibres for thatch and cloth; nuts for food and oils; tree trunks for rubber, balata, gums and resins. Chicle from Zapota tree milk makes chewing gum.
Gathering needs little capital and low technology; yield per person is very low and little or no surplus is produced.

example.q: Why is gathering unlikely to be important in the global economy?
steps: It uses very low technology and little capital.
Yield per person is low and there is hardly any surplus to sell.
Synthetic substitutes of better quality and lower price have replaced many gathered products.
example.answer: Low yield, no surplus and competition from synthetic products

learn.reallife: Tribal communities in Jharkhand and Odisha collect tendu leaves, mahua and sal seeds; cooperatives like TRIFED help them sell these forest products.

learn.hook: Every summer, Gaddi shepherds in Himachal drive thousands of sheep up to high meadows; every winter they bring them down. This ancient rhythm has a name — transhumance.
points: After hunting, people learned to domesticate animals; pastoralism may be subsistence (nomadic herding) or commercial (livestock rearing).

Nomadic herding or pastoral nomadism is a primitive subsistence activity: herders depend on animals for food, clothing, shelter, tools and transport, moving with their livestock for pasture and water.
Animals vary by region: cattle in tropical Africa; sheep, goats and camels in the Sahara and Asiatic deserts; yak in Tibet; llamas in the Andes; reindeer in the Arctic and sub-Arctic.

Three main regions: (1) the core region from the Atlantic shores of North Africa eastwards across the Arabian peninsula into Mongolia and Central China; (2) the tundra region of Eurasia; (3) South-west Africa and the island of Madagascar.

Transhumance: seasonal migration from plains to mountain pastures in summer and back to the plains in winter — e.g. Gujjars, Bakarwals, Gaddis and Bhotiyas in the Himalayas. Pastoral nomadism is declining due to political boundaries and new settlement plans.

example.q: A Bakarwal family in Jammu moves its goats to the high pastures of Kashmir in April and returns in October. Explain the movement.
steps: Summer: plains get hot and dry; mountain pastures are green → move up.
Winter: mountains get snow-covered → move down.
This seasonal vertical movement is transhumance.

learn.reallife: Raika camel herders of Rajasthan and Gaddi shepherds of Himachal still practise pastoralism, though grazing land is shrinking.

learn.hook: New Zealand has about five sheep for every person! Its fenced ranches export wool and meat worldwide.
points: Commercial livestock rearing is more organised and capital intensive than nomadic herding; it is associated with western cultures and practised on permanent ranches.

Ranches cover large areas divided into parcels fenced to regulate grazing; when one parcel is grazed, animals move to another (rotational grazing). The number of animals is kept within the pasture's carrying capacity.
It is a specialised activity rearing one type of animal — sheep, cattle, goats or horses; meat, wool, hides and skin are processed and packed scientifically and exported to world markets.
Emphasis on breeding, genetic improvement, disease control and health care.
Important countries: New Zealand, Australia, Argentina, Uruguay and the USA.

example.q: Give three differences between nomadic herding and commercial livestock rearing.
steps: Nomadic: subsistence, moving herds; commercial: market-oriented, permanent ranches.
Nomadic: many types of animals kept; commercial: one type of animal (specialised).
Nomadic: little capital or science; commercial: capital intensive with scientific breeding and disease control.
example.answer: Subsistence vs commercial; mixed vs single animal; low vs high capital and science

learn.reallife: India's dairy and poultry giants use scientific breeding and veterinary care, borrowing practices from commercial livestock rearing.

learn.hook: In Mizoram's hills, smoke rises from burning forest patches in March. It's not a wildfire — it's jhum cultivation.
points: Agriculture is practised under many combinations of physical and socio-economic conditions, giving different farming systems.
Subsistence agriculture: the farming area consumes all, or nearly all, of the produce grown locally. It has two types: primitive and intensive.
Primitive subsistence agriculture or shifting cultivation is practised by many tribes in the tropics, especially in Africa, South and Central America and South-east Asia.

Vegetation is cleared by fire and ashes add to soil fertility (slash and burn); patches are small and tools primitive (sticks, hoes); after 3 to 5 years the soil loses fertility and the farmer shifts. The jhum cycle shortens as fertility falls and population grows.
Regional names: Jhuming in north-eastern India, Milpa in Central America and Mexico, Ladang in Indonesia and Malaysia.

example.q: A farmer clears a hill patch by fire, grows rice and maize for 4 years, then moves to a new patch. What are the advantages and problems?
steps: Advantage: ash fertilises soil, little capital needed.
Problem: soil loses fertility after 3–5 years.
Problem: as population grows, fallow periods shorten, causing deforestation and soil erosion.
example.answer: Cheap and simple, but leads to short fallow cycles, deforestation and soil erosion

learn.reallife: Nagaland and Meghalaya still have large areas under jhum; schemes promote settled terrace farming and agroforestry as alternatives.

learn.hook: A family in West Bengal grows two or three crops a year on less than one hectare. How can tiny farms feed so many?
points: Intensive subsistence agriculture is found in the densely populated regions of monsoon Asia.

Type 1 — dominated by wet paddy: very small holdings due to high population density; family labour; intensive use of land; little machinery; farmyard manure maintains fertility. Yield per unit area is high but labour productivity is low.

Type 2 — dominated by crops other than paddy: where relief, climate or soil do not suit paddy, crops like wheat, soyabean, barley and sorghum are grown in northern China, Manchuria, North Korea and North Japan; irrigation is used.
In India, wheat is grown in the western Indo-Gangetic plains and millets in drier parts of western and southern India under this system.

example.q: Why is labour productivity low but yield per hectare high in wet-paddy farming?
steps: Many family members work on a very small plot.
Intensive care, manure and multiple cropping give high output per hectare.
But the output divided among many workers gives low output per worker.
example.answer: Many workers on small plots → high yield per area, low per worker

learn.reallife: In the Ganga delta, farmers grow aus, aman and boro rice crops in a single year — classic intensive subsistence farming.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

learn.hook: Assam's tea gardens began under British planters in the 1830s. Today, a cup of Assam tea is drunk across the world.
points: Plantation agriculture was introduced by Europeans in their colonies in the tropics.
Plantation crops: tea, coffee, cocoa, rubber, cotton, oil palm, sugarcane, bananas and pineapples.

Characteristics: large estates, large capital investment, managerial and technical support, scientific methods of cultivation, single crop specialisation, cheap labour, and a good transport system linking estates to factories and export markets.

Examples: French — cocoa and coffee in West Africa; British — tea in India and Sri Lanka, rubber in Malaysia, sugarcane and bananas in the West Indies; Spanish and Americans — coconut and sugarcane in the Philippines; Dutch — once a monopoly over sugarcane in Indonesia; some coffee fazendas in Brazil are still managed by Europeans.
Today most plantations are owned by governments or nationals of the countries concerned.

example.q: List four characteristics that make a Darjeeling tea estate a plantation.
steps: Large estate under one management.
Single crop specialisation (tea).
Large capital, scientific methods, factory on site.
Cheap labour and transport links for export.
example.answer: Large estate, single crop, high capital and science, cheap labour with export transport

learn.reallife: India is among the world's top tea producers; Kerala's rubber and Karnataka's coffee estates also follow the plantation model.

learn.hook: On Canada's Prairies, a single combine harvester can cut wheat across fields that stretch to the horizon.
points: Extensive commercial grain cultivation is practised in the interior parts of semi-arid lands of the mid-latitudes.
Wheat is the principal crop; corn, barley, oats and rye are also grown.
Farms are very large (roughly 240 to 16,000 hectares), so all operations from ploughing to harvesting are mechanised; there is low yield per acre but high yield per person.
Regions: Eurasian steppes, Canadian and American Prairies, Pampas of Argentina, Velds of South Africa, Australian Downs and Canterbury Plains of New Zealand.

example.q: Compare yield per acre and yield per person in Prairie wheat farming and Bengal paddy farming.
steps: Prairies: huge farms, few workers, machines → low yield per acre, high per person.
Bengal: tiny farms, many workers, intensive care → high yield per acre, low per person.
example.answer: Prairies: low per acre, high per person; Bengal: high per acre, low per person

learn.reallife: India imports and exports wheat on world markets where prices are set largely by farms in the Prairies, Pampas and Australian Downs.

learn.hook: A Danish farm grows barley and fodder, keeps pigs and cows, and sells both crops and bacon. That's mixed farming.
points: Mixed farming is found in highly developed parts of the world: north-western Europe, eastern North America, parts of Eurasia and the temperate latitudes of southern continents.
Farms are moderate in size; crops include wheat, barley, oats, rye, maize, fodder and root crops.
Fodder crops are an important component; crop rotation and intercropping maintain soil fertility.
Equal emphasis on crop cultivation and animal husbandry; cattle, sheep, pigs and poultry provide the main income along with crops.
High capital expenditure on farm machinery and buildings, extensive use of chemical fertilisers and green manures, and the skill and expertise of farmers.

steps: Fodder feeds the farm's animals.

learn.hook: Milk has no holiday: cows must be milked every single day of the year. That's why dairy farming never has an off-season.
points: Dairy farming is the most advanced and efficient type of rearing milch animals.
It is highly capital intensive: animal sheds, storage for fodder, feeding and milking machines; special emphasis on cattle breeding, health care and veterinary services.
It is highly labour intensive because of rigorous care in feeding and milking; there is no off-season as in crop farming.

It is practised mainly near urban and industrial centres that provide a neighbourhood market for fresh milk and dairy products; transport, refrigeration, pasteurisation and preservation have increased storage time.
Three main regions of commercial dairy farming: north-western Europe (largest), Canada, and south-eastern Australia, New Zealand and Tasmania.

example.q: Why is dairy farming located near cities, and how has technology changed this?
steps: Milk is perishable; cities give a nearby market for fresh milk.
Refrigeration, pasteurisation and transport extend storage time.
So dairy products can now travel farther.
example.answer: Perishability ties it to cities; refrigeration and pasteurisation extend reach

learn.hook: Italian olives, Spanish oranges and French wines — the Mediterranean is the world's fruit bowl.
points: Mediterranean agriculture is highly specialised commercial agriculture, practised on either side of the Mediterranean Sea (southern Europe and north Africa from Tunisia to the Atlantic coast), southern California, central Chile, south-western South Africa and south and south-western Australia.
This region is an important supplier of citrus fruits.

Viticulture (cultivation of grapes) is a speciality; the best quality wines come from high-quality grapes; inferior grapes are dried into raisins and currants. The region also produces olives and figs.
Advantage: valuable crops such as fruits and vegetables are grown in winter, when demand is high in European and North American markets.

example.answer: Mild winters let them supply cold markets when demand is high

topics.title: Market gardening, truck farming and factory farming

learn.hook: Tulips cut in the Netherlands in the morning sit in flower shops in Paris, London and Berlin by evening. Welcome to market gardening!
points: Market gardening and horticulture specialise in high-value crops — vegetables, fruits and flowers — solely for urban markets.

Farms are small and located where there are good transport links to urban centres with high-income consumers; it is both labour and capital intensive, using irrigation, HYV seeds, fertilisers, insecticides, greenhouses and artificial heating in colder regions.

Well developed in densely populated industrial districts of north-west Europe, north-eastern USA and the Mediterranean; the Netherlands specialises in flowers and horticultural crops, especially tulips, flown to major European cities.
Truck farming: where farmers specialise in vegetables only; the distance of truck farms from the market is governed by the distance a truck can cover overnight.

Factory farming: a modern development in industrial regions of Western Europe and North America; poultry and cattle reared in stalls and pens, fed on manufactured feedstuff, supervised against disease; needs heavy capital for buildings, machinery, veterinary services, heating and lighting, with breed selection and scientific breeding.

example.q: A farm 300 km from Delhi grows only tomatoes and cauliflower and sends them by truck every night. What type of farming is this, and what limits its distance?

Distance is limited to how far a truck can travel overnight.
example.answer: Truck farming; limited by the overnight truck distance

learn.hook: In Denmark, practically every farmer belongs to a cooperative. In the old Soviet Union, farms belonged to the collective. Two ways of farming together!
points: Farming can also be classified by how farms are organised — owned by farmers individually, by the government, or run as cooperatives or collectives.

Cooperative farming: a group of farmers voluntarily pool their resources into a cooperative society for more efficient and profitable farming; individual farms remain intact. Societies help procure inputs, sell products at favourable terms and process produce cheaply.
The cooperative movement, over a century old, succeeded in western European countries like Denmark, the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden and Italy; in Denmark practically every farmer is a member.
Collective farming (Kolkhoz): based on social ownership of the means of production and collective labour; introduced in the erstwhile Soviet Union to improve efficiency and achieve self-sufficiency.

In a kolkhoz, farmers pooled land, livestock and labour but kept very small plots for daily needs; the government set yearly targets and bought produce at fixed prices; surplus was distributed among members or sold; after the Soviet collapse these farms were modified.

example.q: Give two differences between cooperative and collective farming.
steps: Ownership: cooperative — individual farms remain intact; collective — social ownership of means of production.
Joining: cooperative — voluntary pooling; collective — state-organised with government targets and fixed prices.
example.answer: Private vs social ownership; voluntary vs state-directed

topics.title: Mining: factors, methods and exam practice

learn.hook: Why do we name entire eras of history — Copper Age, Bronze Age, Iron Age — after minerals? Because minerals changed everything.
points: The importance of minerals in human history is shown by stages like the Copper Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age; large-scale mining began with the Industrial Revolution.

Factors affecting the profitability of mining: physical factors — size, grade and mode of occurrence of the deposits; economic factors — demand for the mineral, technology available, capital to develop infrastructure, and labour and transport costs.
Surface (open-cast) mining: easiest and cheapest for minerals close to the surface; overhead costs like safety precautions and equipment are relatively low; output is large and rapid.

Underground (shaft) mining: for deep ores; vertical shafts are sunk and galleries radiate to the minerals; needs lifts, drills, haulage vehicles and ventilation; risky — poisonous gases, fires, floods and caving in cause fatal accidents.

Developed economies are retreating from mining, processing and refining because of high labour costs; developing countries with large labour forces are becoming more important, and several in Africa, South America and Asia earn over half their export income from minerals.

example.q: A mineral deposit lies 600 m deep, is high-grade and in demand, but the region has no roads. Which method would be used, and what may delay mining?
steps: Deep ore → underground (shaft) mining.
Favourable: high grade and demand.
Unfavourable economic factor: lack of transport needs large capital for infrastructure.
example.answer: Shaft mining; transport and infrastructure costs may delay it

learn.reallife: Coal India runs huge open-cast mines in Jharkhand and Odisha, while some older collieries in Jharia use underground shafts — and face fire risks.
